articles.titleOriginal: Mattel Spotlights ‘Barbie in the Nutcracker’ with 25th Anniversary Celebration
articles.summaryOriginal: The rollout includes new dolls, Netflix specials, and more, celebrating the beloved film. The post Mattel Spotlights ‘Barbie in the Nutcracker’ with 25th Anniversary Celebration appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: In 2001, Barbie made her feature-length debut with Barbie in the Nutcracker , setting the stage for another two decades of animated Barbie adventures. As the film turns 25 this year, Mattel is celebrating with new toys, television specials, and more for fans of all ages.

Leading the celebration is an all-new Barbie in the Nutcracker television special. Coming to Netflix this November, the animated special puts a new spin on the beloved 2001 classic, this time casting Barbie “Malibu” as Clara and Barbie “Brooklyn” as the Sugar Plum Fairy. On their adventure to rescue Ken the Nutcracker, the friends will travel through a variety of enchanted lands, face off against the mischievous Rat King, and discover that if kids truly believe in themselves, magical things can happen.
Celebrate 25 years of 'Barbie in the Nutcracker' with a new television special. | Source: Mattel
The re-imagined 'Barbie in the Nutcracker' will air on Netflix this November. | Source: Mattel
Relive the magic of the original 2001 film. | Source: Mattel
Tim Curry returns as the voice of the Rat King's Father. | Source: Mattel
Discover the magic of friendship. | Source: Mattel

The ballet is also getting some more modern moves, thanks to dance legend Debbie Allen . As the special’s co-executive producer and choreographer, Allen created unique numbers that blend classical dance with today’s hip hop, all set to music by Macy Schmidt. The late Tim Curry also returns to the voice cast as the Rat King’s Father, the natural progression of his appearance as the Rat King in the original.

But families don’t have to wait until November to return to the Land of Sweets. The classic 2001 Barbie in the Nutcracker is now available to stream on Netflix, so parents who grew up with the original Clara and the Sugarplum Princess can share the magic of the film that kicked off more than two decades of animated adventures with a new generation of fans.
Barbie Nutcracker Clara and Sugar Plum Fairy 2-Pack. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Nutcracker Ballerina and Chelsea Snow Fairies. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Nutcracker Land of Sweets Horse and Sled. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Sugar Plum Fairy and Clara Deluxe Doll. | Source: Mattel

The anniversary celebration continues off-screen with a new Barbie in the Nutcracker toy collection. Available now at major retailers, kids can re-create the classic story with dolls inspired by Clara, Daisy, the Sugar Plum Fairy, Land of Sweets ballerinas, Chelsea Snow Fairies, and more, complete with poseable bodies that mimic real ballet positions. Each doll features a variety of enchanting accessories and outfits, and select toys can even magically transform their tutus with a twirl.

Nathan Baynard, Vice President and Head of Barbie, Mattel , said, “At Barbie, we’re proud to create stories that inspire imagination and spark joy across generations. As we celebrate the 25th anniversary of Barbie in the Nutcracker , this collection honors the enduring magic of dance and storytelling while inviting today’s families to create new holiday traditions and memories together.”

The original Barbie in the Nutcracker is now available to stream on Netflix, with the re-imagined special joining it this November. To learn more and shop the new dolls, visit mattel.com .

articles.titleOriginal: Your face gets antiaging science. Now what?
articles.summaryOriginal: Core Biogenesis and Faravelli are testing whether the biotech behind facial skincare can be scaled up to treat the rest of the body. There’s a jar sitting on a lab bench in Strasbourg that isn’t for sale. That’s kind of the point. Core Biogenesis built it, alongside its Italian distribution partner Faravelli, purely to make […] The post Your face gets antiaging science. Now what? appeared first on

bodyOriginal.text: Core Biogenesis and Faravelli are testing whether the biotech behind facial skincare can be scaled up to treat the rest of the body.

There’s a jar sitting on a lab bench in Strasbourg that isn’t for sale. That’s kind of the point. Core Biogenesis built it, alongside its Italian distribution partner Faravelli , purely to make an argument: that the same biotech doing serious work on faces could do just as much for the rest of the body, if anyone bothered to formulate it that way.
They’re calling it Skin Longevity Butter.

The gap it’s pointing at is a real one. Facial skincare has spent the past several years absorbing genuinely advanced science, lab-grown growth factors, barrier-repair peptides, actives with actual clinical trials behind them. Body care mostly hasn’t kept pace. A body butter is still, for most people, a body butter: something that moisturizes and smells nice. Core Biogenesis wanted to know what happens if you stop treating that as a given.

Two ingredients do the heavy lifting: Peauforia and Peauvita, proprietary biomimetic growth factor technologies Core Biogenesis developed using its own plant-based production platform [ 1 ]. In plain terms, they’re lab-made compounds engineered to behave like the growth factors skin already produces to repair itself, encapsulated in tiny lipid capsules called oleosomes that help carry the actives where they need to go. None of that would matter much if the formulation didn’t also feel like something people would actually want to use, so the team paired those actives with Illipe butter and a supporting lipid blend, aiming for a texture rich enough that the science doesn’t announce itself.
Tony Abboud, Chief Commercial Officer at Core Biogenesis, frames the logic simply.

“As skincare routines extend beyond the face, biotechnology offers an opportunity to create body care that supports skin quality, resilience and longevity,” he said. “Skin Longevity Butter provides a glimpse into what that future could look like.”

Skin Longevity Butter isn’t a one-off. It’s part of a wider Longevity Concepts collection the two companies have built together, which also includes a Lip Longevity Gloss and an Eye Longevity Shadow, both running the same growth-factor approach into color cosmetics rather than skincare proper. Taken together, the collection reads less like a product launch and more like a pitch deck aimed at other brands: here’s what’s possible if you’re willing to formulate around it.

That pitch lands at a moment when longevity has become one of beauty’s most reliable growth stories, no longer confined to the premium skincare shelf and increasingly showing up in hair care, body care, and now makeup. Ingredient suppliers have noticed, and they’re building the technology platforms to match.

None of it gets to a shelf, though, without a middleman most shoppers never think about. Faravelli distributes ingredients and helps brands turn a formulation concept into something a factory can actually produce at scale, work that sits well outside where most of the credit in a beauty launch usually lands. Deals like this one hint at distributors doing more of that translation work themselves rather than waiting for a brand to ask.

Whether Skin Longevity Butter itself ever shows up on a shelf is almost beside the point. The concept behind it, using biotechnology to get skin to repair and renew rather than simply sit under a layer of moisture, is where the industry’s longevity story seems to be heading next: fewer products built to hide what aging looks like, more built to interrupt it at the source. If body care follows the path facial skincare already took, the ingredient panel on a body butter may soon read a lot more like the one on a serum.

articles.titleOriginal: Your gut just joined the official aging checklist
articles.summaryOriginal: A new industry analysis maps 30-plus microbiome startups against longevity, and finds a field still torn between wellness and medicine. For a long time, the gut microbiome sat in the “probably relevant, hard to prove” bucket of aging science. That changed, officially at least, in 2023, when the widely cited framework describing the hallmarks of […] The post Your gut just joined the official aging

bodyOriginal.text: A new industry analysis maps 30-plus microbiome startups against longevity, and finds a field still torn between wellness and medicine.

For a long time, the gut microbiome sat in the “probably relevant, hard to prove” bucket of aging science. That changed, officially at least, in 2023, when the widely cited framework describing the hallmarks of aging, the biological processes researchers broadly agree drive us toward decline, expanded from nine categories to twelve. Gut dysbiosis, the breakdown of a healthy microbial balance in the digestive tract, made the cut. It’s now considered a driver of aging in its own right, not just a symptom of it.

A new landscape analysis from Plug and Play Ventures , a firm that scouts startups across health and biotech, takes stock of what’s actually being built in response. The team mapped more than 30 companies working at the intersection of microbiome science and longevity [ 1 ]. What comes back is a field with real scientific momentum and, frankly, a still-unresolved identity crisis.

Some of the underlying biology explains why investors keep circling back here. About 70% of the human immune system lives in the gut. Roughly 90% of the body’s serotonin, the neurotransmitter tied to mood, gets produced there too, not in the brain as most people assume. And unlike a person’s genome, the microbiome is something people can actually change through diet, lifestyle and now, increasingly, through targeted intervention.

The market has followed the science, more or less. According to the Microbiome Global Market Report 2026 , the global microbiome market grew from $295 million in 2020 to more than $800 million in 2025, and it’s projected to top $3 billion by 2035. Diagnostics, the tests that tell you what’s going on in your gut, still make up more than 80% of that market today. But therapeutics and active microbiome modulation, the products that try to actually change what’s happening rather than just report on it, are the fastest-growing slice. The field, in other words, is moving from measuring the problem to treating it.

The report organizes the startup landscape around four biological “levers,” though the lines between them blur more than any tidy framework suggests. Inflammaging, the chronic low-grade inflammation that builds quietly over decades, is the best understood of the four, tied to a weakened gut barrier that lets bacterial fragments leak into the bloodstream and trigger a slow-burning immune response linked to heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Metabolic health is the best-funded corner by a wide margin. Companies like Viome and Pendulum have raised hundreds of millions of dollars around the idea that gut bacteria shape how the body handles blood sugar and energy, a story that’s picked up extra relevance now that GLP-1 drugs dominate the metabolic conversation.

The gut-brain axis might be the most surprising piece of all this. Research published in Nature in 2024 found distinct microbiome signatures showing up years before the clinical symptoms of cognitive decline appeared, which raises the odd possibility that the gut functions as an early warning system for conditions like Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. Then there’s the gut-skin axis, probably the least expected connection on the list, linking intestinal inflammation to visible aging: everything from eczema to accelerated collagen breakdown. It’s part of why L’Oréal, Unilever, and Estée Lauder have all quietly built out microbiome research programs of their own.

Worth remembering here: this isn’t the field’s first attempt. Kaleido Biosciences shut down in 2022. Evelo Biosciences closed in 2023. Seres Therapeutics, despite winning FDA approval for its therapy Vowst, ended up selling it to Nestlé Health Science in 2024 rather than commercialize it alone. The common thread, according to the report, is that these companies treated the microbiome as a single, isolated drug target, when it actually behaves as an interconnected system touching inflammation, metabolism, brain function and skin, more or less all at once. Newer entrants, armed with better sequencing and AI-driven modeling, are betting they can finally treat it that way instead.

One company the report singles out is Jona, a New York-based platform founded by Leo Grady, who previously led the AI pathology company Paige.ai to its first-ever FDA approval for an AI diagnostic product. Jona’s real difference isn’t the testing itself, but what happens after. Its AI cross-references a person’s results, which can flag more than 21,000 different microorganisms, against roughly 220,000 peer-reviewed studies, then simulates how different diets or supplements might shift that person’s biology before recommending anything.
“We’re seeing a real inflection point in consumer interest around the microbiome,” Grady said, noting that nearly half of Americans now report taking probiotics daily or almost daily [ 2 ].

Still, the report is candid that most startups in this space haven’t fully committed to a longevity positioning yet, leaning instead on general wellness claims or narrow disease indications. That’s starting to shift. Whether it shifts fast enough, and whether these companies end up getting judged by clinical trial data instead of gut-health marketing copy, is probably the question that decides which ones are still around in five years.

articles.titleOriginal: Next Generation Longevity heads to Osaka
articles.summaryOriginal: NGL 2026 will bring clinicians, scientists, founders and investors together to turn healthspan ideas into clinical action. Next Generation Longevity 2026 will convene in Osaka, Japan, on 15–16 October, bringing together an international group of clinicians, researchers, founders, technologists and investors to examine how longevity medicine can move from a rapidly expanding body of knowledge […] T

bodyOriginal.text: NGL 2026 will bring clinicians, scientists, founders and investors together to turn healthspan ideas into clinical action.

Next Generation Longevity 2026 will convene in Osaka, Japan, on 15–16 October, bringing together an international group of clinicians, researchers, founders, technologists and investors to examine how longevity medicine can move from a rapidly expanding body of knowledge into clinical and commercial practice. The inaugural two-day meeting will take place at Nakanoshima Qross, Osaka’s government-backed regenerative medicine innovation hub, with a program spanning precision medicine, biomarkers, applied AI, regenerative therapeutics and the business of healthspan.

Co-chaired by physicians Anant Vinjamoori and Deepti Agarwal, alongside Japan-based healthcare executive Naoko Kita, NGL 2026 has been deliberately designed as a relatively small, curated gathering rather than a conventional sequence of lectures and exhibition booths. Debates, fireside conversations, workshops and case-based Boardrooms will put different disciplines around the same problems – with implementation, rather than information alone, as the intended endpoint. The organizers’ own ambition for the gathering is not a modest one: they describe it as something like the World Economic Forum for longevity and the future of medicine – a global, cross-disciplinary room where debates and working Boardroom sessions take on some of the field’s most pressing open questions, in the hope that what surfaces there changes how the field actually operates, rather than simply how it talks about itself.

Longevity.Technology: Longevity science is hardly suffering from a shortage of information; the harder problem is what happens when that information leaves the paper or podium and encounters patients, clinical practice and economics. Translation increasingly demands different priorities in the same room – scientists asking what the evidence supports, clinicians what can responsibly be done and founders, investors and policymakers what can actually be built and scaled. Consensus may be comfortable, but structured disagreement is often more useful; NGL’s Boardroom format is interesting precisely because it is designed to pressure-test assumptions rather than manufacture agreement. Longevity medicine now sits at the collision point between frontier science and ordinary life, where biomarkers must inform decisions, AI must improve rather than decorate practice and regenerative medicine must make the difficult journey from possibility to application. Conferences are rather good at producing conversations – and business cards; the more meaningful measure is what survives the flight home. NGL’s emphasis on prototypes, partnerships and plans speaks to what the sector increasingly needs: not simply more knowledge about extending healthspan, but better ways of putting the useful parts to work.

The idea took shape on a trip to Japan. Co-chair Dr Anant Vinjamoori visited a year ago to give a talk and came away struck less by the country’s stem-cell science and regenerative medicine frameworks than by something harder to put on a slide: a culture in which longevity is simply how people live, day to day, rather than a frontier being pioneered. That distinction, worked through with the other co-chairs Dr Deepti Agarwal and Naoko Kita, became the seed of NGL – the conviction that the setting itself should be part of the argument, not just its backdrop.

The format also developed in response to the organizers’ experience of attending longevity conferences themselves. They saw value in bringing a young and unusually multidisciplinary field together, but felt that successive keynotes and conventional panels could leave participants with plenty to think about and rather less to do. Their response is a meeting intended to make the room itself part of the program – small enough for participants to contribute rather than simply observe, with connections curated around what individuals are trying to achieve.

Central to that approach is the NGL Boardroom, a business-school-style case format in which physicians, scientists, entrepreneurs, policymakers and investors work through unresolved decisions in longevity medicine. Clinical evidence may pull in one direction while technological feasibility, economics or regulation pulls in another; consensus is explicitly not required.
A core faculty will return across multiple sessions rather than appearing for a single presentation, allowing arguments to develop over the two days.
Brian Kennedy (Director, NUS Centre for Healthy Longevity)
NUS Academy for Healthy Longevity cofounder and director Andrea Maier
Makoto Kuro-o of Jichi Medical University,
Precision medicine physician Florence Comite
Kenji Shibuya , CEO of Medical Excellence JAPAN
Pat Caroll (Global Chief Medical Officer of Hims)
Yoshiki Sawa (Chairman of Nakanoshima Qross, Cardiovascular surgeon and President of Japanese Society of Regenerative Medicine)
Anthony Molina (co-lead, Central Laboratory and Biorepository for XPRIZE Healthspan)
Raghav Sehgal (Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree and Faculty Member at Yale University)

Japan is more than a convenient pin on the conference map. Its population longevity and aging demographics make it an important real-world case study for healthspan medicine, while its regenerative medicine ecosystem offers a different perspective on how emerging therapies can progress toward clinical use. The organizers see the country as a potential bridge between international longevity medicine and a developing Asia-Pacific ecosystem.

The venue makes that argument rather literally. Nakanoshima Qross brings clinical care, R&D and an international forum together on one site; the conference will therefore discuss translational medicine within an infrastructure designed around translation rather than in the more familiar habitat of a hotel ballroom.

There is a cultural dimension too. The program sets regenerative therapeutics, precision diagnostics and AI alongside Japanese approaches to food, purpose and social connection. Accompanying experiences include matcha and fermentation traditions, with an optional post-conference study tour to Nagano complete with traditional Buddhist cuisine, shrine visit, a meeting with the town’s famous ‘Green Centenarians’ and a chance to enjoy the spectacular autumn foliage. The intention is not to confuse tradition with clinical evidence, but to consider healthspan as something lived as well as prescribed – a useful distinction when preventive medicine ultimately depends on what happens beyond the clinic.

The agenda begins with the biology and measurement of aging before moving deliberately toward application. Biomarker sessions will examine what current tools actually measure and where their clinical utility begins to fray; system-focused discussions will consider aging across the brain, heart, gut and endocrine system rather than treating biological age as one conveniently obedient number.

AI receives similar scrutiny. Alongside discussion of tools already scaling in clinical settings, a boardroom session will explore clinical workflow support, patient education and longitudinal personalized care. Regenerative medicine sessions will consider cellular therapies and Japan’s regulatory landscape, while another strand tackles insurance, policy and employer models – the less glamorous machinery through which preventive medicine either becomes part of healthcare or remains an attractive parallel universe.

That question of application extends to biological age testing itself. A dedicated discussion will look at how such testing is actually being used once it leaves the research setting – what incentives it creates for clinicians and patients, and what implementation might look like in practice, including how insurers and employers could build around it.

Two of the summit’s Boardroom sessions bring that tension into sharper relief, and both look likely to produce more than conversation – early indications are that at least one will feed into a published white paper, carrying the argument beyond the room. One puts clinicians and scientists from markedly different backgrounds in the same room to compare how they assess patients, prioritize interventions and decide what does or does not belong in a longevity practice – a reminder that the field is scaling before it has fully agreed on what it is. Another sets a telehealth platform, a consumer health brand and a diagnostics company against each other, each already owning one piece of the patient relationship – testing, prescribing, ongoing care – and each wanting the rest; the session asks whether the more defensible strategy is to compete for that ownership outright or interoperate and split the value, with investors effectively forcing the answer by rewarding whichever model actually returns capital.

NGL’s stated measure of success is what attendees do afterwards. Its organizers want participants to leave with an actionable blueprint, prototype or partnership rather than accumulated notes; follow-up is intended to continue beyond Osaka, including support around individual clinical or business goals.

NGL’s stated measure of success is what attendees do afterwards. In the run-up to Osaka, organizers are collecting each participant’s business goals and the connections they’re hoping to make; after the conference, that will become a personal action blueprint – agreed introductions, useful materials and follow-through on whatever was promised in the room, whether that’s a partnership lead, a research brief or something else specific to the individual. An outcomes desk will then track progress over the following year, making sure those commitments are actually kept rather than left to fade once the flight home lands.

Not gonna lie, it is an ambitious test for a conference – but a useful one. Longevity medicine has become adept at describing possible futures; the more consequential work now lies in deciding which of them can withstand evidence, implementation and the untidy business of becoming ordinary medicine.

bodyOriginal.text: Frederich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.

The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft , or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School , which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.

bodyOriginal.alt: a painting by Frederich Kunath of a landscape with a large cloud at sunrise and the Oasis band logo in the top left corner

bodyOriginal.text: “Sometimes I’m Almost There” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 97.8 centimeters

Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.

As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”
The Nearest Faraway Place continues through October 24. See more on Kunath’s Instagram .

articles.titleOriginal: Fizz Creations Secures Global License for Fuggler
articles.summaryOriginal: Fuggler expands in 2027 with new products across gaming, collectibles, and novelty. The post Fizz Creations Secures Global License for Fuggler appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: Fizz Creations strikes a global licensing deal with Libertas Brands for Fuggler. The company will expand the brand’s product range in 2027, bringing new offerings to key markets.

Starting next year, Fizz Creations will develop and distribute a full Fuggler collection to consumers worldwide. This launch spans key markets across the U.S., the UK, Europe, and international territories. This collection plans to deliver Fuggler branding across a lineup of digital games, collectibles , and pop-culture products.

From kids to kidults, the new range brings a variety of products to consumers. Standout items include Fuggler Fidget Cubes, Fidget Light Keychains, Fart Machines, and Whoopee Cushions. Both the cubes and keychains will feature mystery pack formats with six characters to collect, including a rare Golden Fuggler.

“Securing the global Fuggler licence is huge for us,” says Zoe Ryan, Head of Marketing at Fizz Creations. “It’s proof we’re building toward being a genuine worldwide leader in gaming, pop culture, and social play. The USA is our big opportunity, but this is a global launch, and we can’t wait to get it in front of retailers and fans everywhere from 2027.”

articles.titleOriginal: Can we make the brain age backwards?
articles.summaryOriginal: A new functional brain-age clock is attempting to measure how well the brain is aging and whether interventions can change its trajectory. What if your brain could have its own biological age and, more importantly, what if that number could change? That is the question behind Brain Years, a functional brain-age model developed through a […] The post Can we make the brain age backwards? appeared fi

bodyOriginal.text: A new functional brain-age clock is attempting to measure how well the brain is aging and whether interventions can change its trajectory.
What if your brain could have its own biological age and, more importantly, what if that number could change?

That is the question behind Brain Years, a functional brain-age model developed through a collaboration between neurotechnology company Sens.ai and the Buck Institute for Research on Aging . Rather than looking only at the brain’s structure, the approach asks a more practical question: how well is the brain actually functioning? It is an important distinction. An MRI can show what the brain looks like. A functional assessment tries to understand what it can do.

For Dr Eric Verdin, president and CEO of the Buck Institute, that distinction is central to the wider problem of measuring aging. Traditional medicine tends to tell us whether a measurement falls inside a normal range. Aging science is increasingly interested in something more dynamic: where a person is heading.

“If you’re in the normal range, you know, there’s no taking into account of the trajectory and how close you are to becoming abnormal,” Verdin explains on the latest episode of Longevity.Technology UNLOCKED . That idea of trajectory sits at the heart of Brain Years.

Sens.ai CEO Paola Telfer and her team spent years collecting EEG and performance data from users in real-world settings, rather than relying solely on tightly controlled laboratory conditions. That created a different kind of challenge. Before AI could make sense of the data, the company needed to make sure the data itself was worth trusting.
“We knew that it’s garbage in, garbage out with AI,” Telfer says.

The company developed its own sensors and refined the system to detect when the signal might be compromised; for example, if someone is moving, chewing gum, talking or blinking excessively. The resulting dataset spans people from their early teens to their late 80s. But the real work began after the data had been collected.

The Brain Years model examines hundreds of variables derived from EEG, event-related potentials and performance during standardized tasks. Rather than deciding in advance that one particular brain signal must be the answer, the researchers used machine learning to determine which combinations were most strongly associated with chronological age and functional capacity. The result is a score intended to describe functional brain age relative to chronological age. Think of it less like an odometer and more like a weather forecast. Your chronological age tells you how long you have been alive; a brain-age clock attempts to provide another view of where your brain currently sits and potentially where it is going.

This is where the story becomes more interesting. A clock that merely tells you that your brain is older or younger than expected could be useful, but it would remain largely descriptive. The bigger promise is whether the measurement can track changes following an intervention.

Early data from Sens.ai and the Buck Institute suggests there may be something worth investigating. Telfer says an intervention study showed “5.18 years of reversal on the Brain Years measure after a two-month intervention.” But Verdin is careful about what that means.

“You’ll never hear me claiming that we’ve reverted aging,” he says. The next step, he argues, is a properly designed prospective, placebo-controlled trial that can establish whether the change represents a genuine alteration in brain aging rather than simply an improvement in test performance. That caution matters. An aging clock is ultimately a model built from measurements. If the number changes, the crucial question is whether biology changed with it.

The researchers also want to compare Brain Years with other approaches, including MRI-based clocks and blood-based proteomic measures. In other words, the future may not belong to one definitive aging clock, but to several imperfect windows that collectively give us a clearer picture.
From dementia prevention to everyday brain health

There is also something quietly radical about starting the conversation before dementia. Brain aging is often discussed as though it begins when cognitive decline becomes clinically obvious. Telfer argues for a much earlier intervention point, encompassing issues such as attention, anxiety and burnout. And that opens up a different vision of longevity medicine: not waiting for the brain to fail before measuring it, but tracking function while there is still plenty of room to intervene.

Sens.ai’s commercial path is increasingly focused on clinics, where Telfer sees the technology as a more portable and repeatable complement to expensive imaging and specialist interpretation. Verdin, meanwhile, places it within what he calls “Scientific wellness” – consumer-facing interventions subjected to the kind of scientific rigor usually associated with medicine.
That middle ground could prove important. Longevity has never suffered from a shortage of things people can buy. What it has lacked is reliable ways to determine whether those things work.

The promise of a functional brain clock, then, is not really the number itself. It is the possibility of turning brain health from something we periodically worry about into something we can measure, follow and potentially improve, while there is still time to do something about it.

articles.titleOriginal: Game Store Day Is Growing, and the Tabletop Community Is Ready to Play
articles.summaryOriginal: Excitement is building for Game Store Day as the tabletop industry comes together to celebrate local stores, welcome more players, and create memorable experiences on November 7. The post Game Store Day Is Growing, and the Tabletop Community Is Ready to Play appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: One big day to celebrate the places we play.

On Saturday, November 7, GAMA: The Tabletop Game Association will celebrate the second annual Game Store Day , bringing retailers, publishers, creators, and players together for a day dedicated to the Friendly Local Game Stores at the heart of tabletop gaming.
And if the industry’s response is any indication, year two is shaping up to be a good one.

Game Store Day is a free GAMA member-only initiative created to celebrate and elevate the role independent game stores play in their communities. Inspired by events like Record Store Day and Indie Bookstore Day, the annual celebration spotlights the creativity, diversity, and passion of tabletop gaming and the stores that bring it all together.

Local game stores do a lot more than put games on shelves. They’re where someone learns their first game, discovers their next favorite one, finds a regular gaming group, or sits down across the table from someone who might become a new friend.
Game Store Day gives those stores an opportunity to turn it up a notch.

“Game Store Day is a great excuse for a store to put their best foot forward and create magic and wonder in their space,” said Kylie of Games Unlimited in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. “Get creative with the experiences you offer, and you’ll have an event your customers will be talking about as they patiently look forward to next year.”

bodyOriginal.alt: Game Store Day 2026 Publishers | Source: GAMA

bodyOriginal.text: Game Store Day 2026 Publishers | Source: GAMA
That excitement isn’t limited to retailers.
Game Store Day is designed to bring the tabletop ecosystem together, with publishers, creators, media, retailers, and fans all playing a role in building excitement around local stores.
And publishers have answered the call in a big way.

GAMA has already doubled its publisher participation goal for 2026, bringing even more industry support behind this year’s celebration. Participating publishers are helping create opportunities for players and retailers to discover games, demos, promotional items, and other surprises as part of Game Store Day.
That growing participation is exactly what Game Store Day is about: giving the entire industry a reason to rally around the places where tabletop gaming happens every day.
For stores, that means November 7 is a chance to show off what makes their community special.

Host a tournament. Teach a new game. Break out a demo. Plan something unexpected. Introduce regular customers to something they’ve never played or give someone who’s never stepped inside a game store a reason to pull up a chair.
There isn’t one right way to celebrate Game Store Day. In fact, the best events look different everywhere you go.
RELATED WiT Stories: The Human Shelf: Why Connections Still Wins at Retail
With publisher participation already gaining momentum, it’s time for Friendly Local Game Stores to get involved.

Participating stores will join a coordinated campaign designed to drive foot traffic, increase visibility, and put local game stores at the center of tabletop excitement heading into the holiday season. Game Store Day builds on GAMA-led initiatives like Winter Wishlist by combining industry promotion with grassroots community participation to help players discover games and the local stores that carry them.

GAMA member retailers have until October 8 to register for Game Store Day 2026 and guarantee delivery of a Publisher’s Box. You can register up until Nov. 2 to receive a digital marketing Toolkit. The sooner the better!
So, start thinking about what November 7 could look like in your store. Get creative. Give your regulars something to look forward to. Give somebody a new reason to walk through the door.
And create a little magic while you’re at it.
Register your store and learn more about Game Store Day at gamestoreday.com .

According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture, the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's

bodyOriginal.text: Trapezoidal motifs appear throughout this concrete condominium block in Tokyo , designed by Japanese studio Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture .
Named Shin Nakano Trapezoidal, the five-storey block of 11 residential units was designed for local developer Real Partners.

According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture , the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's location on the Musashino Plateau, a large tableland in western Tokyo.

bodyOriginal.alt: Concrete housing block by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture has completed a concrete condominium block in Tokyo "The Musashino Plateau is one of those landscapes that people live on without ever seeing," said principal architect Ryuichi Sasaki told Dezeen.
"Our challenge was to take something as abstract as a position within a plateau and translate it into a motif that residents encounter every day," he continued.
"[It is] in the facade they walk past, in the shadows on the stairs, in the light that reaches their rooms."

bodyOriginal.alt: Exterior view of Shin Nakano Trapezoidal condos

bodyOriginal.text: Trapezoidal motifs feature throughout the design On the block's eastern edge, a sheltered entrance area is framed by tall, trapezoidal concrete columns and features trapezoidal floor tiles.
A large sliding metal door leads into a lobby and stairwell, where an industrial-feeling steel staircase with grille treads allows daylight to filter through.
This lobby divides the block into three wings across which the apartments are separated, with a combination of single-storey and duplex units that extend into a basement and rooftop terrace.

bodyOriginal.alt: Interior view of condo at Shin Nakano Trapezoidal by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: The five-storey block contains 11 residential units Each apartment takes advantage of views over the street to the south and a park to the north, with large metal-framed windows that slide open for cross-ventilation.
The interiors are deliberately minimal and pared-back, with timber floors, exposed concrete ceilings, white-painted walls and large areas of built-in storage.

Read: Groupwork completes "world-first" high-rise held up by stone exoskeleton The trapezoidal motif was carried through into openings in the interior walls and floors, staircase balustrades and even the floor plan of some rooms.
Externally, the block is finished in exposed concrete, with textured trapezoidal and triangular panels created by embossing the surface of the concrete after it was poured.

bodyOriginal.alt: Condo interior by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: Their interiors have been kept minimal and pared-back "A residential building of this scale is experienced in fragments — an entrance, a stair, a window — so the motif had to work at every one of those moments," said Sasaki.
"We are proud to offer the residents of Nakano a building that connects them, quietly and daily, to the ground it stands on," he added.

bodyOriginal.alt: Bedroom interior at Shin Nakano Trapezoidal housing block in Tokyo

bodyOriginal.text: Each apartment has large metal-framed windows Previous projects by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture include a mixed-use development containing homes and a community performance space in Tokyo, which was housed within similarly angular concrete volumes.
Elsewhere in Tokyo, Kenta Hirayama recently created the steel-clad House in Kinuta and Kenta Sano & Associates combined a glass-fronted dance studio with a house .
The photography is by Takumi Ota Photography .

articles.titleOriginal: Growth Hormone Receptor Antagonism Modestly Slows Aging in Mice
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers here run a much larger than usual mouse study to show a ~10% slowing of aging, depending on how one slices the data, in mice genetically engineered to exhibit a growth hormone mutation that changes the interaction of circulating growth hormone with the growth hormone receptor on cell surfaces. Growth hormone is switched from a receptor agonist (binds with and activates the receptor) to

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers here run a much larger than usual mouse study to show a ~10% slowing of aging, depending on how one slices the data, in mice genetically engineered to exhibit a growth hormone mutation that changes the interaction of circulating growth hormone with the growth hormone receptor on cell surfaces. Growth hormone is switched from a receptor agonist (binds with and activates the receptor ) to a receptor antagonist (binds with the receptor without activating it, blocking other molecules from activating it). This extension of life is entirely expected given all of the long-lived mouse lineages in which growth hormone metabolism is in some way sabotaged . This specific form of sabotage had not been tested rigorously, however. While interesting, it is worth noting that humans with Laron syndrome , an inherited dysfunction of growth hormone metabolism analogous to many of the mouse models exhibiting longevity, do not appear to live meaningfully longer than the rest of the human population.

Interventions that disrupt growth hormone (GH) action are recognized as some of the most potent methods for extending lifespan. Accordingly, GH receptor antagonists (GHA) represent potential therapeutics to improve healthspan . Somavert ( Pegvisomant for injection), used for treating patients with acromegaly , is currently the only FDA approved GHA. This drug was based on our laboratory's early 1990s discovery that mutating a codon for a conserved glycine - at position 119 in bovine GH or 120 in human GH - to a variety of amino acids , including lysine , ultimately converted GH from an agonist to antagonist. Since Pegvisomant has poor affinity to rodent GHR, it has not been tested for its ability to extend lifespan in rodents.

To address this gap, we evaluated survival in GHA transgenic mice, a mouse line that played a crucial role in the discovery and development of Pegvisomant and has been maintained in our lab since 1991. While a prior study with several limitations failed to detect lifespan extension in GHA mice, our current study addressing these limitations shows that both median and maximal lifespan were significantly increased in male and female GHA mice, with maximal lifespan extended by 186 and 265 days, respectively. Analysis of an independent cohort of 2-year-old mice revealed that GHA males and females were less frail with enhanced grip strength despite increased adiposity . These findings demonstrate for the first time that GH antagonism can improve health and extend lifespan.

articles.titleOriginal: Studio Saar tops LDF pavilion with police and rain shields
articles.summaryOriginal: This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression. Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand The post Studio Saar tops LDF pavilion with

bodyOriginal.text: This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression.

Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand outside London's Somerset House and near India House . According to Studio Saar co-founder Ananya Singhal, this location had a significant impact on the project.
"The Strand is right next to Somerset House and right next to India House," Singhal told Dezeen.

"Somerset House is where the British Navy was administered from during the colonial period, and India House is where the Indian High Commission is," he continued. "So this site has a very interesting history behind the relationship between India and the UK."

bodyOriginal.alt: The Pangolin Shield,

bodyOriginal.text: Studio Saar designed The Pangolin Shield pavilion for LDF The Pangolin Shield pavilion also faces a bust of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.
To Singhal, placing the pavilion in this location was an opportunity to underline the new relationship that India has with the UK "and possibly the world", he said.
"We're an Indo-UK practice working with a British engineer, so there was something about this project and the site which kind of brought that combination together," Singhal said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion on The Strand in London

bodyOriginal.text: It is located on a pedestrianised part of The Strand The Pangolin Shield was designed by Studio Saar and structural engineers Atelier One , led by founder Neil Thomas. It was constructed using a bamboo grid shell, which the studios wanted to use because of the material's many positive characteristics.
"It's lightweight, it's durable, it grows very quickly; once you finish with it, it's biodegradable, and you can make super interesting shapes from it," Singhal said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Police shields on the roof of a pavilion

bodyOriginal.text: The roof is made from police shields The gridded shell structure that forms the base – and which is strengthened by steel fastenings – was then covered in two very different types of shields.
On top of the bamboo grid is a first layer, made from traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis, a type of bamboo stick.
This first layer is then covered by knups, woven rain shields that are traditionally used by farmers in the north-east of India.

Read: Studio Saar creates forest-like pavilion at Design Mumbai "The police shields were designed by the British colonial rulers to keep riots down in India all those years ago; it's really beautiful, the idea of making it a part of the structure that shelters both visitors and the locals here," Singhal said.
"The knups are from Meghalaya, the wettest place on Earth – it gets more than two metres of rain per year and its name literally means 'the land of the clouds'," he continued.

bodyOriginal.alt: Rain shields on a pavilion for LDF

bodyOriginal.text: On one side the police shields are covered in rain shields The design of the pavilion, which resembles a creature covered in scales, was also inspired by Singhal's work outside of Studio Saar.

"I'm a wildlife photographer and conservationist, and one of the animals that I hear about a lot is the pangolin, which is the most trafficked mammal on Earth," he explained. "So I wanted to create a structure that brought the pangolin into conversation."

bodyOriginal.alt: Small model of a pangolin

bodyOriginal.text: A model of a pangolin was placed inside the pavilion Inside the pavilion, visitors can admire a sculpture of the pangolin and look at the drawings for the project.
As the pavilion was damaged when it was transported from India to the UK, it will be shown with an interior scaffold during London Design Festival (LDF) due to "abundant caution," Singhal said.
"It's a public space and there are going to be drunk people coming up and down this street", he said in reference to the risk of the pavilion being damaged.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion on the Strand in London

bodyOriginal.text: During LDF the pavilion will be supported with the addition of internal scaffolding Overall, Singhal believes that the project is a good representation of the values that Studio Saar stands for.
"Something which we really hold dear as a practice is the idea you can take small, humble, crafted things and combine them to make amazing things," he said.
"And that's the piece that we've practised in many areas, and what we would really love to do, and that's what we're doing here with the police shields and the knups."
Other projects on show at London Design Festival include Craft x Tech, which explores Japanese craft in a contemporary way, and Lozi's modular plywood furniture .

The Pangolin Shield is on show at The Strand, WC2 1HL, from 12 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.

articles.titleOriginal: Design Academy Eindhoven students reinvent the bathroom for a resource-scarce future
articles.summaryOriginal: Tiles decorated with hair and a dissolving washbasin made of soap are among the student projects featured in Behind Closed Doors, an exhibition by the Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents. The exhibition featured standout projects born from a 10-week educational partnership between the bathroom brand and students of the academy's The post Design Academy Eindhove

bodyOriginal.text: Tiles decorated with hair and a dissolving washbasin made of soap are among the student projects featured in Behind Closed Doors, an exhibition by the Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents.

The exhibition featured standout projects born from a 10-week educational partnership between the bathroom brand and students of the academy's Social Design master's degree that explored the future of the bathroom.

bodyOriginal.alt: Tiles by Sarah Kinzer and Moss A Moschen

bodyOriginal.text: The Behind Closed Doors exhibition included projects by Sarah Kinzer and Moss A Moschen (above) As part of the collaboration, the students were asked to investigate how bathrooms can be reimagined in a more circular way that doesn't just conserve resources but also encourages more circular behaviours and habits in its users.

"We gave them the idea that in a circular world, Kaldewei would not produce a new bathtub anymore because we would reuse our old bathtubs, give them a new surface and build them in again," the company's head of design Christian Büttner told Dezeen.
"So what the students really explored for us was: what are the barriers against this that we have in our head?"

bodyOriginal.alt: Hair bath mat by Carlotta Talkenberger

bodyOriginal.text: Carlotta Talkenberger created a bath mat from human hair Among the eight featured projects, some of the most visceral explored how we can overcome the natural aversion we have against waste materials – especially ones that have passed through the hands of other people.

Design Academy students Sarah Kinzer and Moss A Moschen visited student bathrooms on their street in Eindhoven and documented the traces of use that were left behind – black mould, clumps of hair, limescale on a showerhead.

bodyOriginal.alt: Wash Away Your Guilt by Ian Chu

bodyOriginal.text: Ian Chu's soap washbasin disappears with every use The duo abstracted these patterns in a collection of steel tiles, some even incorporating real strands of their own hair, to find beauty rather than revulsion in the intimate history of these materials.

"We try to make an aesthetic of disgust," Moschen explained. "If we want to talk about circularity, but as a society we hold expectations towards very clean and polished materials, how can we even do that?"
"So I think we just tried to flip the narrative and question what happens when something that we call disgusting is intentionally part of the design language."

bodyOriginal.alt: Reed sculpturesin Behind Closed Doors exhibition by Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents

bodyOriginal.text: Guadalupe Vanini Cervini created sculptures from fallen reeds In a similar vein, Carlotta Talkenberger felted a bath mat from human hair to explore the double standard inherent in using animal hair to make many of the products around us while shunning our own.

And in Ian Chu 's project Wash Away Your Guilt, discarded cooking oil is turned into soap and used to form a washbasin that slowly dissolves with every use, exploring both the practical and moral implications of circularity.
"She was also questioning a little bit if circularity is a concept that we hide behind so we don't feel guilty," Moschen explained.

Read: "Industry in Germany is no longer open to what design can do" say Currents Berlin organisers As Europe's record-breaking heatwaves reduced the continent's water supplies to historic lows , other students shared speculative projects about how limited access to this crucial resource could reshape our habits and spaces.

A satirical film by Hanxiao Xu depicts a community that reuses its bathwater and attributes it with mythical healing properties, while Philipp Hohnerlein and Gabriela Augustyniak imagine that bathing will cease entirely.

Instead, their Bathtube project suggests tapping into the waste heat of data centres and turning their pipes into impromptu hammams, offering the warmth and comfort of a bath without the water wastage.

bodyOriginal.alt: I

bodyOriginal.text: Xinliang Zhou turned everyday objects into shower instruments Nature's resources also take centre stage in a project from Guadalupe Vanini Cervini that explores the indigenous principle of the Honourable Harvest – a " covenant of reciprocity " stipulating how to responsibly take from nature and give back in return.

In this spirit, she used naturally fallen reeds from the wetlands around Eindhoven to create a series of sculptures set within that same landscape, but transported to Berlin for the sake of the exhibition.

Another exploration of more-than-human design came from Tina Lehnhardt , who created a performance around a series of costumes – embodying black mould, moisture, a dead skin cell and a humidity-loving insect known as a silverfish – to humanise the other life forms with which we share our bathrooms.

bodyOriginal.alt: Behind Closed Doors exhibition by Design Academy Eindhoven and Kaldewei at Berlin design festival Currents

bodyOriginal.text: Tina Lehnhardt's costumes represent other life forms in the bathroom Finally, taking a more playful take on the topic, Xinliang Zhou created a simple method and instructions for how to turn everyday bathroom items into musical instruments and every shower into a jam session.
The Behind Closed Doors exhibition formed part of the inaugural Currents design festival in Berlin, which the founders argue is well on its way to establishing itself as Germany's new design capital.
Currents 2026 took place from 10 to 12 September 2026 at various locations across Berlin, Germany. For other design events around the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide .

articles.titleOriginal: "Is touching really asking too much?"
articles.summaryOriginal: Look-but-don't-touch design exhibitions are inherently unfulfilling so it's good that some designers are finding ways to let people properly interact with their work, writes Alice Fisher. In the 1990s as a student in London, I got a summer job at a famous department store. I was a sales assistant for towels and robes working next The post "Is touching really asking too much?" appeared first on Dez

bodyOriginal.text: Look-but-don't-touch design exhibitions are inherently unfulfilling so it's good that some designers are finding ways to let people properly interact with their work, writes Alice Fisher .

In the 1990s as a student in London, I got a summer job at a famous department store. I was a sales assistant for towels and robes working next to the bathroom furniture department which, true to the shop's reputation for ostentatious luxury, included some incredibly ornate toilets.
One morning, word spread around the staff that someone had – somehow – managed to use a display toilet for its intended purpose. Reactions ranged from outraged disgust to amused respect.
I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in
Personally, I was envious – imagine clambering into that sterile room set and settling on the porcelain throne. Even the most prestigious customer wouldn't get away with that.

I'm surprised how often I think about that toilet when visiting design exhibitions these days. Not for any weird reason – the only stool I like to see is one that's handmade, preferably from reclaimed wood – but because I so often want to climb into the displays of beautiful furniture I'm looking at and settle in.
Sadly, at most design festivals that would be as shocking and frowned upon as hopping onto the lav in a department store display.

Read: Five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene Looking but not touching or interacting with design is, to my mind, a strange and impotent experience. I spend so much time staring really intently at chairs trying to imagine what they feel like, when what I really want to do is loll in them.

The two things I overuse the most at London Design Festival (LDF) and other such events are my camera phone – obvs – and the surreptitious finger. You know what I mean – the index finger you slide out at hip height to feel the buttery softness of a leather chair arm, or the cool surprise of a marble tabletop, when the publicist and designer are looking the other way.

Just to be clear, I'm not stupid. I understand the financial and creative investment that studios and designers have put into these displays. I know that most of the furniture on show is a prototype or produced at great personal cost to the maker and that letting the clumsy, feckless public loose on these masterpieces is not a good idea.
Many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way
And yet… wouldn't it be great if there was an idiot-proof version of the furniture you could have a go on?

Cast your mind back over the most discussed or fondly remembered exhibits at recent design weeks and you can see I'm not the only person who feels this way. Paul Cocksedge , Alison Brooks and Waugh Thistleton all made landmark wooden LDF installations in recent years that could be sat on, walked through or even climbed up.

I'm so pleased that the AHEC exhibition Wood for the Trees, which debuted at Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design (3DD) in June , will also appear at LDF this week. The show includes beautiful rocking wooden benches by Benchmark , which are such a great place to sit.

Read: Read LDF edition of Dezeen Dispatch online now! Also at 3DD this year was an outsized conversation pit . This version of the 1950s favourite – in beautiful lemon linen – was a collaboration between furniture brand Vipp and Spanish architecture studio Mesura . Big enough to hold 60 people, visitors were encouraged to slip off their shoes and climb inside using swimming pool-style ladders. Most design critics opted to bounce like toddlers at soft play rather than hold a meaningful conversation, which made the experience even more delightful.

Metamorphosis in Motion by architect Lina Ghotmeh at this year's Milan design week gave a similar thrill. Watching people explore Ghotmeh's magenta maze, which filled the courtyard at the Palazzo Litta, was a pleasure.

The trend for staging shows in apartments rather than sterile showrooms also reflects how many design-week visitors want to experience furniture in a natural way. While design shop Artemest is probably the OG brand for turning fabulous apartments into even-more-fabulous fantasy exhibition spaces during Milan , I think French vintage dealer Antoine Billore's Loreto apartment for perfume house L'Artisan Parfumeur this year was the one in which I really wanted to sit down and pretend it was mine.
"I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."

British designer Charlotte Taylor 's breakout show was Home from Home at 3DD 2025 (pictured). She not only curated this exhibition of work by 40 furniture designers held in an apartment at Noura Residency on Sankt Peders Stræde, but also lived in the space during the design festival.

Recently, Taylor told me that, although the idea was to get away from the "untouchable tableau" of the typical design show, she hadn't expected visitors to get quite so comfortable, quite so quickly in her personal space. "It became a performative piece, to the extent that I'd be filmed by a load of strangers while making coffee in the morning," she said. "It was pretty extreme."
She should have held a lottery that gave visitors the opportunity to apply to spend the night there themselves. I can think of few things that design fans would like more.

All I would like designers to do is think of any way it's possible for visitors to engage with their beautiful creations beyond the look-but-don't-touch of a standard design fair. Using a toilet absolutely crosses the line, but is sitting down, or even touching, really asking too much?
Alice Fisher is a lifestyle journalist based in London. She was previously lifestyle editor at The Observer, and has also written for The Guardian and the Financial Times, among others.

articles.titleOriginal: London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan
articles.summaryOriginal: With London Design Festival underway, we asked long-standing mayor of London Sadiq Khan for his thoughts on the festival and what to see this year. Amy Peacock: Why do you believe London's design scene is worth investing in, and what role does London Design Festival play in this? Sadiq Khan: London has a remarkable history The post London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan app

bodyOriginal.text: With London Design Festival underway, we asked long-standing mayor of London Sadiq Khan for his thoughts on the festival and what to see this year.
Amy Peacock: Why do you believe London's design scene is worth investing in, and what role does London Design Festival play in this?

Sadiq Khan: London has a remarkable history of producing designs that have become global icons. Visionaries such as Thomas Heatherwick and Norman Foster have reimagined architecture and public spaces, while Vivienne Westwood revolutionised fashion with her rebellious designs, and celebrated product designer Tom Dixon and multidisciplinary artist Es Devlin are all showing why London's design is an international success story.

I'm delighted that LDF plays a key role in the success of the industry, showcasing, celebrating and developing our leading talent. The festival is an incredible advert, drawing international attention, investment and visitors as it welcomes more than 600,000 visitors.
I'm hugely proud to support the festival and over the past 10 years have invested £2.2 million that has helped to unlock £1.23 billion for the economy through jobs and investment.
Amy Peacock: What are you looking forward to seeing this year at LDF?

Sadiq Khan: London Design Festival is a huge highlight in the capital's cultural calendar because there are so many great events taking place. There's a lot to look forward to, including The Pangolin Shield, which will be a significant installation on the Strand.

There are design districts that showcase 11 neighbourhoods across the city as local studios, showrooms, galleries and cultural venues open their doors with exhibitions, installations, events and talks, while the V&A continues its long-standing relationship with the festival with Awakenings.

bodyOriginal.alt: The Pangolin Shield at LDF

bodyOriginal.text: The Pangolin Shield by Studio Saar and Atelier One is on display as part of London Design Festival (LDF). Photo by Cajsa Carlson Amy Peacock: How does London's design scene compare to other cities? Do you think it's possible for LDF to have an impact on the scale of design festivals in Milan and Copenhagen, and how does the UK no longer being in the EU have an impact on this?

Sadiq Khan: Our capital is a powerhouse for the creative industries and LDF is a fantastic example of our influence in the design industry. The festival promotes our city's creativity, drawing in the country's greatest thinkers, practitioners, retailers and educators to deliver an unmissable celebration of design. That's why it is one of the world's leading design events and has served as the blueprint for design weeks and festivals globally.

However, there is no doubt that the UK's departure from the EU has made it harder for London's design industry to trade, collaborate and recruit talent across Europe. Increased paperwork, barriers for the movement of creative talent and reduced access to EU funding have brought challenges, but despite all this, London continues to be a thriving and welcoming place for designers.
The top photo of Sadiq Khan is by Caroline Teo

articles.titleOriginal: CircuitPython Goes Turbo With Precompiled Functions
articles.summaryOriginal: It would not be at all original to declare that Python is the new BASIC. Like BASIC, it has been the first programming language for a whole generation of coders, …read more

bodyOriginal.text: It would not be at all original to declare that Python is the new BASIC. Like BASIC, it has been the first programming language for a whole generation of coders, and its main advantage is that it’s quick and easy to write in. Like BASIC it is an interpreted language, and thus rather slow to execute.

Thus while CircuitPython can be very useful for beginners and quick projects, it hits the limitations of the hardware far sooner than it needs to — unless you can pre-compile critical parts of the code, which you now can, thanks to CircuitPython Turbo by [Mikey Sklar] with some help from Anthropic’s Claude LLM.

Now if that sounds a lot like MicroPython’s ‘Viper’ and machine-code compiler, that’s because it is. CircuitPython is a fork of MicroPython with some handy extras on Adafruit boards, but Viper wasn’t one of them until now. Before the Turbo version, CircuitPython only ran in interpreted mode.

Like MicroPython, using CircuitPython Turbo you can flag sections to run as ‘native’, where instructions are compiled but values stay as python objects, which gets you about a 3X speedup. A little more rewriting to declare your variables and pointers and you can use ‘viper’ mode, which can — depending on what you’re up to — result in a 20x to 70x speedup. In Adafruit’s documentation , they demonstrate a Metro RP2040 calculating the Mandelbrot set 3x faster in Native and 19.7 times faster with Viper than normal Python bytecode.

The one thing that we miss from BASIC that CircuitPython Turbo doesn’t give is inline assembly– though interestingly enough, that is in the upstream MicroPython implementation, so perhaps its day will come here too. Not every job is suited to the use of Python on microcontrollers, but we’ve seen it used for everything from e-bikes to a Winamp-inspired music player.

bodyOriginal.text: Designers Bahbak Hashemi-Nezhad and Rafael El Baz have used traditional biscuit moulds to create Sweet Terrain, a collection of wall tiles for a HS2 station made from clay excavated during its construction.

Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz salvaged 12 tonnes of clay dug up from the site of Old Oak Common, a station under construction in London designed by WilkinsonEyre for the high-speed rail network HS2, to make the playful collection.

bodyOriginal.alt: Sweet Terrain tiles

bodyOriginal.text: Sweet Terrain is a collection of wall tiles by Bahbak Hashemi-Nezhad and Rafael El Baz The tiles have distinctive reliefs made with moulds modelled on wooden tools traditionally used to create Ma'amoul – cookies originating in the Arab world. The design draws on the designers' visits to patisseries in west London belonging to Middle Eastern bakers who migrated from Lebanon and Syria.
It is hoped to shine a light on their stories and help bring place-based identity and connections to local communities into the vast and controversial HS2 project.

bodyOriginal.alt: Biscuit-like tiles

bodyOriginal.text: Their design draws on traditional bakeries in West London "The goals were to make hyper-local objects that resonate with those who would ultimately see and use them, and in doing so instil a sense of pride and embed narrative that isn't possible with off-the-shelf products," Hashemi-Nezhad told Dezeen.

"Beyond the resourcefulness and circularity of the project, we wanted to create something meaningful, literally from the bottom up, by engaging local communities and embedding the work for the generations that follow them," added El Baz.
"Infrastructure projects, however large or small, can be humanised and made culturally resonant through design."

bodyOriginal.alt: Old Oak Common construction site

bodyOriginal.text: Each tile is made from clay excavated from the construction site of a HS2 station According to the designers, the Sweet Terrain tiles are set to be used in the station's "quiet spaces", such as multi-faith zones, toilets and corridors.
The exact number of tiles that will be used is yet to be confirmed, but Hashemi-Nezhad said the number will be in the thousands.

bodyOriginal.alt: Sweet Terrain tiles

bodyOriginal.text: Their designs emulate Ma'amoul cookies. Photo by Michael Gardiner Sweet Terrain's initial design process began by diverting 12 tonnes of construction soil from landfill. It was then smoothed and refined, forming the ideal consistency for tile making.
Production was carried out with Craven Dunnill Jackfield – one of Britain's oldest and last remaining traditional tilemakers, which has previously created tiles for London Underground.

Read: London Underground waste repurposed into tiles for tube stations Together with Craven Dunnill Jackfield, the duo developed 3D scans of the biscuit moulds to form the tiles, which have been made in various sizes and depths to ensure optimal style for installation in the public realm.
"Too shallow and it loses its tactility; too proud and it risks chipping and damage due to vandalism," said Hashemi-Nezhad.

bodyOriginal.alt: Ma

bodyOriginal.text: These biscuits are traditionally made with wooden tools Now the designers are working with the manufacturer's glaze lab to experiment with different colour and texture finishes.
However, they are set on using hand-dipped glazes, which they believe will help add a "human touch" to the wider infrastructure project.

bodyOriginal.alt: Sweet Terrain tiles

bodyOriginal.text: The tiles will eventually be used in Old Oak Common station. Photo by Michael Gardiner The bakers with whom Hashemi-Nezhad and El Baz have consulted on the project have described the work as "an act of recognition".

"When these tiles enter the public realm in the new station, it will bring so much joy and pride to us bakers, as well as our communities and families," baker Vasken Jermakian of Sweetland Bakery said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Baker that inspired Sweet Terrain tiles

bodyOriginal.text: Local bakers described the project as "an act of recognition". Photo by Michael Gardiner The HS2 network has been highly controversial, for reasons including its environmental impact on the Chilterns – an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) through which it cuts.
Dezeen recently published construction photos of Old Oak Common station , for which the tiles are being made. Once complete, it will be one of the largest transport interchanges in the UK.
Designer Hashemi-Nezhad is currently a designer in residence at CCA Tashkent, which recently opened its hub within a "basilica-like" tram depot overhauled by Studio KO in the Uzbekistan capital.

articles.titleOriginal: We Are Pi's ads for Interrail break free from travel cliches to show how passengers really feel
articles.summaryOriginal: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style. Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not...

bodyOriginal.text: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style.

Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not a bulldozer or screaming infant in sight? Check. Catchy yet ultimately bland and empty slogan? Check? Smiling, impossibly attractive people? Check.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with that. Holidays for most of us are just a welcome break from everyday life, and a little bit of fantasy never did anyone any harm. And I've got nothing personally against impossibly attractive people; some of my best friends count among their number.

But if you're trying to sell consumers on something they wouldn't normally do, and in fact might be nervous of doing in a foreign country where they don't speak the lingo, you'll need to work a little harder.

That's exactly the challenge that the global brand consultancy We Are Pi , working with social agency Butterfly Effect , were presented with. They were approached by Interrail B.V, the Dutch company behind the European rail travel scheme that makes it cheap and easy to travel across the continent with a special pass.

As well as boosting the scheme, there was also a bit of brand housekeeping to do. Up until this point, Interrail B.V. had two brands for essentially the same rail pass: Interrail for people living in Europe, Eurail for visitors from elsewhere. The latter needed to be folded into the Interrail brand, following the business changing its name from Eurail B.V. to Interrail B.V. earlier in the year.

Better than flying The campaign indirectly challenges the notion that because flying is quicker, it's better. Instead, it leans into the idea that the longer journey isn't an inconvenience; it's part of the adventure, via a brand concept they've dubbed The Interrail Effect.

This was backed up by a customer survey in which around 70% of Interrail customers said their trip changed how they see the world. A similar number considered the experiences more impactful than other types of travel, and around a quarter considered it much more impactful than other holidays they'd taken.

bodyOriginal.alt: Yellow train route with text labels forming the phrase "Realising the best bit is between here and there and there" overlaid on a map of Europe for Interrail campaign

bodyOriginal.text: To get this across visually, the launch poster shows a stylised map of Europe. Running across it is a single yellow line representing a train route; only the stops aren't cities – they're words. Joining them together gives you the sentence: "Realising the best bit is between here and there."
It's a common design trick, but it works because it forces the reader to make a bit of an effort. Had the sentence been instantly legible, it wouldn't make half as much impact.

There's a nice extra touch too: the journey doesn't end with the last word; the line continues, albeit it's now dotted and straight. It's a subtle way to evoke the idea of exploring and making it up as you go along, without beating people over the head with the idea.

Creator-led campaign Another element of the campaign is a series of short video clips made by 30 creators from the US, Canada, Australia and Europe, who were asked to travel across the continent with Interrail over summer and share their experiences.

These clips sit in a comfortable space between standard YouTube shorts and glossy, cinematic films. The former would have been a bit "So what?", the second would have seemed a bit overblown for a target audience that's likely to be sleeping in the cheapest hostel. The sweet spot they've reached feels, in the words of Goldilocks, just right.
Ultimately, there's nothing particularly new in this campaign, but at the same time, there didn't need to be.

As Özlem Birkalan, chief brand and commercial officer at Interrail, puts it: "'The Interrail Effect' isn't something we invented. It's something travellers have described to us for decades, in their own words, after every journey. What's changing is that we're finally building the brand around it. Not around where people travel, but around what travelling like this does to them."

The campaign launched globally on 10 September in the UK, Australia and the US, and will roll out across a mix of paid, owned and earned channels including paid media, organic social, EDM, partnerships and PR as well as participating creators' own Instagram, TikTok and other social platforms.
